analysis.title: Americas Communications Technology: 2026 bus tour takeaways: 650 Group, ANET, CSCO, SMCI
key_insights: GS hosted a hardware and networking investor bus tour in California on 11/19/2026 with 650 Group (private), Arista (ANET, Buy), Cisco (CSCO, Neutral) and Super Micro (SMCI, Sell).

Scale-up is largely embedded and proprietary today. 650 Group expects disaggregated architectures and Ethernet to gain share over time, and sees scale-up Ethernet as potentially the largest networking opportunity.

650 Group expects disaggregated scale-up to become larger than embedded scale-up as servers move to sidecar switch racks and optics run directly from compute into the switch. That broadens the opportunity to ANET, CSCO and JNPR, with ANET best placed in disaggregated scale-up/scale-across and CLS in embedded racks such as NVL72 and AMD Helios.

650 Group expects Ethernet to eclipse NVLink in scale-up over the longer term, and sees OCS as complementary because it lets operators resize domains and reconfigure clusters without recalling the fleet.

AI infrastructure is becoming more heterogeneous, open and network-intensive, with a broader mix of GPUs and custom ASICs and multiple network domains (scale-up, scale-out, scale-across). GS sees the added complexity as supportive of vendors differentiated in silicon, software and system engineering, including ANET and CSCO.

Neocloud outcomes are bifurcating. 650 Group sees the weakest third of operators under increasing pressure, while leaders have become materially more technically capable over the last 3-6 months and can deploy white box and optimize their own architectures. 650 does not expect this to eliminate branded vendors, and cites CRWV pursuing white box for cost-optimized workloads while continuing to deploy Dell elsewhere.

650 Group has not cut its outlook for about 30 GW of US IT power in 2027/28 (roughly 40-45 GW globally). It attributes the gap to chip-vendor expectations to a 6-12 month lag between accelerator shipment and capacity coming online, not to warehousing of GPUs or switches.

650 Group says AI clusters are moving from effectively one network to 3-4 distinct networks, and compute cost rises from roughly $30bn/GW for Rubin to about $120bn/GW for Feynman-generation systems. It argues operators have less incentive to compromise on the network as accelerator spend grows.

SMCI is diversifying into enterprise through CPU-based infrastructure (notably financial services), partnerships with NTNX, CSCO and NTAP, services and software, and a direct sales build-out, and is selling full AI factory/pod-level solutions.

SMCI sees durable cloud/neocloud demand. Its 44% customer from F1Q has communicated aggressive expansion plans, though SMCI is not that customer's sole supplier. Management says customer quality has improved after tighter underwriting of offtakers, financing and data-center readiness, and it has walked away from deals where funding, land/power or the shell was not ready.

SMCI is tightening working capital by matching inventory commitments to customer readiness and using more customer prepayments on larger deployments. Management describes the customer base as better funded and more willing to prepay.

CSCO says CPO is incremental and not a major threat to pluggable optics. The larger hurdle is the lack of a mature ecosystem to assemble advanced silicon and optics at scale. OSFP and connector advances give Cisco a path to 3.2T pluggables, and CPO becomes more compelling where power or faceplate density makes pluggables impractical, such as scale-up.

CSCO does not see CPO as cannibalizing optics because scale-up is served mostly by copper today. Optics are the same technology for DCI, metro and scale-across, so differentiation sits in silicon and network architecture. Effectively 100% of hyperscaler DCI is now served by pluggables rather than transponders.

CSCO says Silicon One's co-development of silicon, systems, hardware and software is a key differentiator in webscale AI, allowing integrated or disaggregated sales. Cisco's long-term ambition is to move essentially its whole networking portfolio onto Silicon One, including service provider and enterprise.

ANET says EOS's advantage is a single 20+ year-old code base across the portfolio. Customers qualify one software image (versus 200+ at competitors in one example), bugs get a common patch, and in-service upgrades matter more in Campus as security patches become more frequent.

ANET says its single code base results in fewer CVEs and consistent patching across the installed base. Management also highlights network segmentation to limit blast radius, and says it is too early to say security drives incremental demand.

ANET does not meaningfully participate in scale-up today. Pilots and testing are expected in 2027 and production ramps in 2028+, partly dependent on next-generation networking silicon. Of three scale-up models, management favors custom co-engineered hyperscaler solutions, which could preserve its targeted 60%-64% gross margin. It does not think commoditized rack-scale switching fits its margin profile.
GS rates ANET Buy with a $240 12-month target (33x NTM+1Y EPS), CSCO Neutral with $115 (18x NTM+1Y EPS), and SMCI Sell with $35 (5.5x NTM+1 EPS).

market_movers.rationale: Best placed in disaggregated scale-up/scale-across, with 2028+ production ramps expected and custom co-engineered hyperscaler designs seen as the best fit for its 60%-64% gross margin target. Target is 33x NTM+1Y EPS.
CPO is seen as incremental to optics and Silicon One is a differentiator. Target is 18x NTM+1Y EPS.
Management cites durable cloud/neocloud demand, better customer quality and enterprise diversification. GS keeps its Sell with a target of 5.5x NTM+1 EPS.

sector_views.rationale: GS sees rising architectural complexity and networking intensity in AI clusters as supportive of vendors differentiated in silicon, software and systems, including ANET and CSCO.

earnings_insights: No earnings results or estimates are given. ANET's 2025 revenue concentration is cited as META 16% and MSFT 26% of total revenue.
risk_factors: ANET: slower cloud capex, customer concentration (META 16% and MSFT 26% of 2025 revenue), competition from Cisco, Huawei, H3C and white box, margin pressure from enterprise sales investment and supply chain costs, pricing pressure from commoditization, and execution risk in enterprise/campus and SD-WAN.
CSCO: competition from Huawei, H3C and white box, margin dilution from more cloud customers, supply chain costs, pricing pressure and dilutive acquisitions.
SMCI upside risks to the Sell: stronger AI server demand, market share gains, core operating margin improvement and customer diversification.
Weakest third of neoclouds are under increasing pressure.

tension_points.bull_case: Leading neoclouds are becoming more technically sophisticated, and their more complex infrastructure makes networking more strategic for vendors. 650 does not expect white box to eliminate branded vendors.
tension_points.bear_case: The weakest third of neoclouds is increasingly challenged, and leaders can deploy white box and optimize their own architectures. CRWV could use white box for cost-optimized workloads.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Leading neoclouds shifting more workloads to white box instead of splitting them with branded vendors such as Dell.

theme_stances.key_argument: Disaggregated architectures and Ethernet are expected to gain share in scale-up over time, broadening the opportunity for ANET, CSCO and JNPR.
theme_stances.evidence: Ethernet to eclipse NVLink in scale-up

theme_stances.key_argument: The weakest third of neoclouds is increasingly challenged while leaders become more technically sophisticated.
theme_stances.evidence: weakest third of the neocloud universe is increasingly challenged

theme_stances.key_argument: CSCO sees CPO as incremental to optics because scale-up is mostly copper today, and pluggables have a long runway.
theme_stances.evidence: CPO is incremental; pluggables have a long runway.
